A.explanation: Too small by about $10^7$. It results from an area error such as using diameter in $\pi d^2$ without halving and converting $\text{mm}$ incorrectly.

B.explanation: Too small by about $10^6$. It comes from using the $0.42 \text{ mm}$ diameter as radius or mishandling the $\text{mm}$ to $\text{m}$ conversion in the wire area.

C.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 4. It is close to the value obtained if diameter is used in place of radius when calculating $A = \pi r^2$.

D.explanation: Correct from $v = I/(nAq)$ with $A = \pi(0.21 \times 10^{-3})^2$, giving about $3.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

hints: Notice the wire is given by diameter $0.42 \text{ mm}$, so first find the radius in $\text{m}$ and then the cross-sectional area $A = \pi r^2$ in $\text{m}^2$.
Connect current to electron flow with $I = nAvq$, where $n = 8.0 \times 10^{28} \text{ m}^{-3}$ and $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Rearrange to $v = I/(nAq)$, substitute $I = 0.57 \text{ A}$ and your $A$, and check the power of ten gives $10^{-4} \text{ m s}^{-1}$ order.
walkthrough: Identify the governing relation for drift speed: $I = nAvq$, so $v = I/(nAq)$ with $n = 8.0 \times 10^{28} \text{ m}^{-3}$, $I = 0.57 \text{ A}$ and $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

Calculate the wire cross-sectional area from the $0.42 \text{ mm}$ diameter. Radius $r = 0.21 \text{ mm} = 2.1 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$, so $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (2.1 \times 10^{-4})^2 \approx 1.39 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$.
Evaluate the denominator: $8.0 \times 1.39 \times 1.60 \approx 17.8$ and $10^{28-7-19} = 10^2$, so denominator $\approx 1.78 \times 10^3$.
Divide: $v \approx 0.57 / 1.78 \times 10^3 \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m s}^{-1}$, with unit $\text{m s}^{-1}$ as required. This is option D.
